Fascicle 55. Above, within the exposition on skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) by means of the two meanings of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the first section has been divided according to ten points.
The explanation of the meaning of "distinct matter" is now complete.
This concludes the first interpretation of the names of the four aggregates,
which first summarizes what preceded and introduces what follows.
This continues up to the establishment of the characteristics as appropriate.
Second is the explanation.
Within this, first, the names of the four aggregates (*skandha*) are individually explained by means of ten gates.
Subsequently, the three natures and the four aggregates are all explained through nine gates.
Regarding the former,
first, the characteristic of the single mind is explained as established in the second fascicle of the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
Among these, two separate sūtras are cited that do not belong to the *Maulī Bhūmi*.
The first sūtra begins with "As the Blessed One said," and so forth.
The second sūtra begins with "Furthermore, as it is said," and so forth.
The following explains the scriptural text. Jing says:
"From those of such a kind, up to those who give rise to even a single thought of the mind."
Regarding the meaning of "arising":
that which is subsumed within the continuity of the presently arising mind is called "producing a single mind.
This explains that the first cited scripture refers only to producing a single mind.

Furthermore, following the subsequent explanation, it is stated through a pure mind that, according to the conventional principle of continuity, one utters a single word and performs a physical action.
This interpretation applies to the first sutra regarding a single utterance; how much more so for physical and verbal actions, which are practiced in accordance with the measure of one's own mind.
Master Ji said:
"In this context, based on the conditions, the measure of the duration of as many moments as constitute the object of focus is termed 'one mind.
It does not mean that a single momentary consciousness is called 'one mind.'"
Second, it clarifies that the conceptualizing mind (*manas*) and the non-conceptual five consciousnesses share the same present objects as their conditions.
There are three reasons for explaining these causal conditions:
first, extreme clarity.
Because that mental consciousness (manovijñāna) perceives the present object simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, it apprehends the object with distinct clarity.
Second, because of its attention (*manasikāra*) toward that [object]:
fundamental attention intends to grasp the present object.
The mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses takes those same forms as its object.
This is due to the two supports mutually nourishing one another;
that is to say, the support of that mental consciousness is the mind-faculty (*manas*), which is precisely the *manas*[-consciousness].
Secondly, there is also nourishment based on the eye faculty;
because that visual consciousness relies on the eye to perceive forms,
it causes the mental consciousness to apprehend its objects with clarity.
Therefore, the eye faculty also provides nourishment to that mental consciousness;
hence it is said that "the two supports provide nourishment. Ji (基) says:
As stated in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya-nyāyamukha-śāstra*:
"The five consciousnesses are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is likewise."
Now, among these, the five consciousnesses are manifest direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
they are not called "conceptual" because they do not associate with vitarka, vicāra, and so forth.
Although the sixth [consciousness] shares the same objects as the five [sensory consciousnesses],
it is called "conceptual" (*savikalpa*) because it is associated with vitarka and vicāra; thus,
it is said to share the same objects as the present.
It can be clearly understood that if the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) follows those five sensory consciousnesses, it is not clear,
because it takes the past as its object.
For instance, when one contemplates events spanning hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they are not clearly perceived;
this has been refuted in the fifty-first fascicle.
Now, since this first reason states that [the object] is "extremely clear," [it is untenable].
Just as clarity is obtained by taking the present as an object,
the five consciousnesses do not obtain clarity by taking the past as an object.
Since the second cause [the mental attention] occurs simultaneously with the five [consciousnesses], it directs its attention toward the objects of those five.
Therefore, it is known that [the object] also serves as a condition for the present.
Regarding the third cause, which consists of the two supports that provide nourishment:
visual consciousness has four supporting faculties (*indriya*).
The mental consciousness has five supporting faculties:
four are the same as those of the eye-consciousness, with the addition of its own [faculty] as the fifth.
This means that the mental consciousness must rely on two supports—its own faculty and the eye faculty—and be nourished by them before it can take the present as its object.
If one relies solely on the self as a basis,
then the apprehension of objects will not be clear;
this refers to the state of distraction, not to the internal state of meditative concentration.
This refers to the apprehension of objects by means of the eye as a gateway, which is termed "nourishment" (āhāra);
it does not mean that the visual consciousness itself is termed "nourishment" because it relies upon the sense organ.
Furthermore, just as the arising of wholesome or unwholesome cognitions regarding the eyes and so forth must necessarily be induced by the mind (*manas*) before they can occur.
Because the mental faculty supports visual consciousness, there can be wholesome and unwholesome states;
thus, one comes to know that the mind and the eye share the same object.
Third, the correspondence with afflictions is explained.
The self-nature of the mind-king is inherently pure;
it is only due to association and the persistence of latent tendencies that it becomes profound. Jing said:
Among the Hinayana treatises, the Vibhajyavāda school of the Vātsīputrīyas takes this meaning as its tenet within the Mahayana;
therefore, they state that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure (*cittaprakṛti-prabhāsvara*).
Because it is obscured by adventitious defilements,
it is described as impure; later, when one is free from these obscurations, [it is pure].
One further attains pure speech. Question:
Regarding the statement that the "ground" (bhūmi) binds the mind, among the two types of causes for defilement, which should it be called? Answer: It should be called "associated" (saṃprayukta).
Both the primary and secondary afflictions, when they manifest in the present, are termed "entanglements" (paryavasthāna).
Regarding the question, "What herein is said to be the respective latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) up to the state of insecurity (*an-astaṃbhya-tā*)?",
this passage explains that the seeds of affliction are termed *dauṣṭhulya* (coarseness) and the state of insecurity.
Because those seeds of affliction render the body and mind incapable of functional flexibility (*akarmanyatā*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter eleven, states:
"Mundane meditative absorption (*laukika-dhyāna*) can only sever and abandon the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to that category, but it does not extract the seeds."
That text explains that the power of the seeds of affliction which lacks functional capacity within the body and mind is called *dauṣṭhulya*.
Furthermore, it refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) up until the moment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) as suffering.

This is said because, being possessed by the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), tainted formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) lack autonomy and cause those formations to be unstable, thereby constituting suffering.
The following passage explains that one should contemplate suffering as being like poison, heat, an abscess, and so forth.

The *Vitarkabhūmi* explains that regarding [suffering] like a poisonous, inflamed ulcer, applying hot ashes which increases its pain is called the contemplation of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhata*).
Regarding it as a poisonous, inflamed ulcer, applying a cooling medicine which produces a slight, subtle pleasure is called the contemplation of change-as-suffering (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhata*).
"Just as a poisonous, inflamed abscess is by its very nature the contemplation of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Jì (基) says:
"In this context, it is taught that when the mind arises, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is pure."
This is based on the fact that what is not inherently defiled is called "pure," rather than being pure because it is untainted (*anāsrava*);
this is the same as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The fourth [category] consists of the three defiled afflictions (*saṃkliṣṭa*).
The first refers to unwholesome karma;
the second refers to mental distress and physical suffering, as these correspond to the lower realms.
Regarding the basis of suffering, there is only suffering and no sorrow;
this third stage thus pervades all three realms.
The fifth [stage] clarifies bondage.
Jingyun: The seeds of affliction that follow along and bind are called the mental bond of affliction.
Delighting in various activities such as preparing robes and alms bowls, which obstruct the cultivation of the Noble Path,
is called the bondage of karma.
Furthermore, regarding the three places, even up to what is called the mind of renunciation:
Attachment to birth and death obstructs the mind of renunciation that seeks liberation;
it thus obstructs the wholesome qualities conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśala*).
This applies even to one who finds joy and pleasure in attaining deliverance.
The roots of goodness, such as "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and the others, arise within meditative concentration;
they are associated with joy and bliss,
and serve as the skillful means for attaining the Noble Path and liberation.
The unwholesome karma of the desire realm can obstruct those three kinds of wholesome states.
For one who has attained the Noble Path,
it directly obstructs the very essence of the Noble Path that has been attained.
Furthermore, karma that accords with maturation is also called "karmic entanglement," namely:
karma leading to the miserable realms and karma pertaining to Uttarakuru.
The karma of the non-percipient heavens (*asaṃjñisattva*) and so forth;
furthermore, the karma of wrong aspirations (*mithyāpraṇidhāna*) and so forth refers to aspiring to become a nāga, a garuḍa, or the like.
Furthermore, regarding the various non-Buddhist practitioners who seek the karma for rebirth in the heavens and so forth,
when categorized separately there are six types, but when combined in total there are four;
the first is those who delight in and are attached to worldly activities (*karmārāma*).
Second, karma that acts as an obstacle in three locations;
third, karma conducive to maturation (vipāka);
fourth, karma of wrong aspiration.
This constitutes four [categories].
Within the second, three are opened up;
thus, by distinguishing their names, there are six.
Tai said: First, the mind of renunciation is called the "mind of renunciation.
Second, one gives rise to a mind of joy and delight toward renunciation.
Third, regarding the attainment of the noble path:
since the first two [types of joy] are themselves the skillful means for the noble path,
one does not establish the joy of mind and pleasure regarding the attainment of the noble path itself.
Baso said: "Renunciation and joy—this is the life of a renunciant.
If the dharma of renunciation is indeed the preparatory stage for the path of seeing."
The sixth [section] clarifies the universal and object-specific mental factors (*sarvatraga* and *viniyata*).
First, the question and answer introduce and enumerate them; second, their characteristics are distinguished;
third, their functions are clarified.
Regarding the subsequent analysis of the four objects:

within the analysis of their characteristics, it says "the provisionally established object-condition" (*prajñaptālambana*), where "provisionally established" (*prajñapti*) refers to names and expressions (*nāma-pada*).

Regarding "that which is grasped through provisional combination": this refers to grasping at provisional images and appearances. Regarding "the characteristics of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with verbal expression": [this refers to the habitual tendencies that underlie linguistic discourse].
This means that one is unable to discern conceptualizations such as names and so forth;
rather, there are only verbal expressions whose seeds persistently follow along and provide nourishing perfuming,
causing various types of conceptual discrimination to arise accordingly.
Regarding "experiencing accordingly":
whenever it encounters any object, it immediately experiences it.
Next, the function is explained.
Ce says: The preceding section distinguished the specific characteristics;
here, karma is distinguished in relation to its results.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth are called the cause,
because the mind is the effect.
Thus says Ki.
In this context, what is the function of contact (*sparśa*)?
It has the function of serving as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).
As in other places, such as the *Abhidharmapada*, it is stated that [contact] is solely the basis for feeling; why then is it not said to be the basis for perception and volition as well?
Regarding the distinction between this and that:
this refers to the general theory that all [mental factors] depend upon contact (*sparśa*),
because attention (*manasikāra*) arises immediately after contact.
If one considers them according to their sequential operation, there is only feeling (*vedanā*).
As for the function of feeling: it serves as the basis for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding its function, this means that cravings for objects and so forth all arise only subsequent to feeling.
The following clarifies the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
They arise from four types of objective entities, namely those that are desirable and so forth;
this refers to the basis of desire (*chanda*).
"Certainty" refers to the basis for resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*);
"habitual practice" refers to the basis for mindfulness (*smṛti*); and "investigation" serves as the basis for both.
As stated in the treatise:
The seventh [section] clarifies the three minds of initial encounter, seeking, and determination;
these are of the same category as those preceding them.
Herein lies the intended meaning of the question:
This refers to the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) among the mental concomitants (*caitta*) that are dissociated from mind (*viprayukta*).
These phenomena arise from the moment of the sudden,
initial mind (*ābhoga-citta*) up until the time of the decisive mind (*niścaya-citta*).
The answer says:
"It arises immediately according to the mind.
Why, in this context, is it stated that the first three minds are the standard, while the fourth and fifth are not mentioned?
Each point of reflection is also included within the questions.
Furthermore, the nature of the preceding mind is definitely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); the universal, the object-specific, and the indeterminate [mental factors] are likewise [indeterminate].
Regarding the four categories and three natures, there may be cases where they arise simultaneously with other wholesome factors, afflictions, and so forth.
If a wholesome or unwholesome mind arises, it necessarily co-arises with these factors;
this principle is certain.
Because the universal [mental factors] and so forth are not determined to be of a single nature,
this section asks only about these; therefore,
it asks only about the first three minds and does not include the latter two.
The eighth question: As the sūtra says, "up to their distinctions.
This cites the sūtra.
Why is it that when those dharmas mature with distinct characteristics, they are described as being in union without distinction?
Question: Since the nature and characteristics of the various minds and mental factors are each distinct,
why is it said that they cannot be analyzed apart and that their conjunction is without differentiation?
Answer: It arises only when a multitude of factors combine and support one another;
its capacity to experience and comprehend an object is only fully realized through such cooperation.
To be incomplete by one [factor] is called "undifferentiated.
These are four alternative names for the ninth mental factor.
Why is it called "concomitance" (*saṃprayoga*)? The answer is: "by way of equality of entity" (*vastu-samatā*), and so forth.
Regarding this, Qingbian (*Ji*) says:
"Equality of entity refers to the substance (*svabhāva*)."
Because their essence is entirely one,
there is no second [entity] such as feeling and so forth.
As for "the bases and so forth":
This means that they function with respect to the same object and location.
Furthermore, it is because they depend upon the same basis, conditions, location, and so forth.
Regarding "time and so forth":
Because they occur at the same moment.
Regarding "the activity is the same," it means that the activity performed proceeds toward the same object.
It is like taking blue as the condition for [the perception of] blue.
Furthermore, there are those produced by the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. Jing says:
Why is it that the aspects of the practice (*ākāra*) are not described as being "equal"?
The explanation states:
within the Mahāyāna, when describing the aspects of the practice, one cannot say they are equal.
Why is this so? Practice is the aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga),
while characteristics are the aspect of appearance (nimitta-bhāga).
This means that when the mind and mental factors apprehend an external object, their various modes of discernment (*darśana-bhāga*) differ;
based on these, the manifold distinctions of the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the discernment arise.
Therefore, one cannot say that speech and action correspond, and so forth.
Tai says: "Or perhaps it is spoken of in certain contexts."
They are divided into two:
the mutual identity of karma and so forth.
The meaning of "concomitance" (saṃprayoga) is explained through four types of equality.
This refers to the difference between opening and closing [the categories].
Regarding the explanation of "possessing activity" (*savyāpāra*):
for instance, the eye-consciousness, the mind (*citta*), and its mental factors (*caitta*) all collectively apprehend a single objective essence (*vastu*).
Each, with respect to a single object of focus, gives rise to many modes of engagement;
each transforms its own image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) as arising from its own mind,
which is termed "evolving through immeasurable varieties of mental aspects."
Regarding "having a basis," Jing says: "For example,
a single visual consciousness arises by relying upon three faculties."
First is the eye faculty;
second is the mental faculty (*manas*) that arises and ceases in succession;
third is the defiled faculty derived from the manas in the distant past.
The same applies to the other consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is said that by means of a single category, the name "having a support" (*sāśraya*) is applied to all that which serves as a basis. Question:
If that is so, since all conditioned phenomena such as form arise only by having a basis upon which they rely, then material phenomena must also have a basis; why, then, do you say they do not?
This is now explained for the sake of clarity.

Although there are no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) that lack a basis, the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*) as it is used here refers to the faculties (*indriya*) being designated as the support.
Other material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) that do not arise in dependence upon the sense faculties are not called "having a basis" (*sāśraya*).
Jì (基) says: this means that mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth, being of the same category as consciousness, rely upon a physical support (*āśraya*).
Just as visual consciousness relies upon the eye faculty,
so it is with the mental factors that arise simultaneously;
the rest may be understood by analogy.
The opponent raises an objection to refute [the argument], saying:
"Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), which ones do not have a basis?
For what reason are mental factors (*caitasika*) and so forth alone designated by that name?"
Therefore, it is generally said:
although there are no conditioned phenomena that lack a basis,
this is not the sense of "basis" established in this context.
Because those self-causes are not constant supports;
furthermore, because associated and coexistent dharmas are not constant supports.
Only that which is constantly a support serves as the measure for this support.
The eye and so forth are the "bases" (āśraya) for consciousness and its associates, and not for other phenomena.
Alternatively, the term "basis" refers to the six classes of consciousness which depend upon their respective sense-faculties as their supports.
Since the consciousness that depends [upon it] receives its name from its basis,
it is said to "constantly depend" [on it];
this interpretation is superior.
The tenth [section] clarifies five pairs of mutually opposing phenomena:
first, the opposition between suffering and pleasure; second, the opposition between suffering and pleasure on one hand and equanimity on the other.
Third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] corresponds to that ignorance;
fourth, knowledge corresponds to ignorance;
fifth, knowledge corresponds to nirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement that "the answer is because [equanimity] acts as an associate to all feelings and all afflictions, being mutually opposed to them," Jing says:
"The feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā) is universally associated with all other feelings and afflictions."
Ignorance is likewise; it is associated with all afflictions, and because their meanings are equivalent, they are paired together. Ji says:
That which acts as an auxiliary to all feelings is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
That which acts as an auxiliary to all afflictions is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Feeling acts as an auxiliary to feeling.
Afflictions serve as companions to afflictions;
therefore, it is said that they face one another.
Furthermore, both sensation and ignorance can act as the companions to the affliction of sensation.
Therefore, these two are explained in relation to one another.
By this textual evidence, it is proven that within the fourth dhyāna, the factors of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*) are not established as distinct branches (*aṅga*).
Thus concludes the tenth section, which provides a comprehensive analysis of the names of those four aggregates (*skandha*).
From here below is the second section, which takes the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) as a general framework to subsume the four formless aggregates (*ārūpya-skandha*),
forming a chapter that provides a detailed analysis through nine gateways.
Within this, the first part groups the four aggregates into the three natures.
That is to say, regarding all things without distinction:
the four aggregates are all common to the three natures;
there is no distinction such that some are common while others are not.
Next, one verse is cited to list nine categories:
first, the basis;
second, the intrinsic nature.
1. The three associations; 2.
the four conventional [truths] and so forth;
3. the weak and so forth.
Six matters;
seven distinctions;
eight gains and losses.
Ninth, the "Treatable and the Counteractive.
This section analyzes the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) across nine gates,
consisting of three parts.
First, the wholesome aggregates are analyzed through nine gates.
First, the bases of reliance are clarified as having six periods;
these will be distinguished in detail below within the explanation of the third gate, the "Conjunction" (saṃprayoga) gate.
The second [section] clarifies intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Within the Mahāyāna, all eleven [wholesome factors] are considered intrinsically wholesome (*svabhāva-kuśala*);
this differs from the *Vibhāṣā*, which holds that only shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), and the three roots of goodness (*trikuśalamūla*) constitute intrinsic wholesomeness.
In the third *Saṃprayoga*,
according to the sixty-ninth [verse],
among the eleven wholesome factors, only *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is excluded.
The remaining ten types are present in all wholesome minds.
As stated in the third fascicle of the first volume:
"How many [factors] depend exclusively on wholesome states and not on all places of mind-arising, yet exist in all stages and not at all times?"
Answer: Faith and so forth,
with non-harming as the final member.
Furthermore, the fifty-third [fascicle] states:
"Wherever there is shame (hrī), there must be remorse (apatrāpya);
wherever there is remorse, there must likewise be shame."
Although there are various differing explanations,
we now take the sixty-ninth [treatise] as definitive:
if it occurs within meditative absorption, it necessarily arises together with eleven [mental factors].
When a wholesome mind arises within the indeterminate stage (*aniyata-bhūmi*), it necessarily arises together with ten mental factors, excluding *praśrabdhi* (pliancy).
The present statement regarding their presence or absence during the six periods refers to those whose functional power is particularly strong.
The fifty-third [fascicle] states that "there may be shame (kṛti) without necessarily being bashfulness (hrī)"—this is also based on their functional dynamics.
Since bashfulness is shame toward oneself, while shame is shame toward others:
if one feels shame for having committed an offense, one will necessarily feel shame toward others as well.
One may naturally feel shame for others but not necessarily feel shame for oneself.
If one were to determine the presence or absence [of these qualities] based on their essential nature rather than their relative status,
then it would also have to be admitted that wherever there is lack of self-respect (*āhrīkya*), there must necessarily be lack of decorum toward others (*anapatrāpya*).
Regarding the necessity of having shame based on the existence or non-existence [of an object],
in the fourth section concerning the provisional and the real,
if one follows the *Abhidharmapitaka* (First Scroll), it says:
Non-delusion has as its essence the discernment arising from the wisdoms acquired through birth, hearing, reflection,
and cultivation; its function is the rejection of evil.
This passage seems to state that non-delusion (*amoha*) is merely nominal,
because it derives its essence from wisdom (*prajñā*) among the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).
The Tripiṭaka Master says:
The mention of "concordant wisdom" (*samyag-prajñā*) reveals the essence of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Since non-delusion as a root of goodness is not included among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*),
we know that there is a separate textual source for it.
The textual explanation states that these three factors are provisional.
In the fifth chapter, the "Threefold Analysis," it is taught that the roots of goodness belonging to the non-concentrated stages constitute the inferior level.
In the world, mundane wholesome states are considered middling,
while the untainted (anāsrava) are superior.
Within the untainted wholesome states, those that first sever the higher afflictions are designated as lower.
Next, the abandonment of intermediate afflictions is called "middle," and the subsequent abandonment of lower afflictions is called "upper.
These are now explained together.

Therefore, it is said that "inferior grade" refers to the wholesome roots belonging to the various non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), or the untainted wholesome roots (*anāsrava-kuśala-mūla*) in the concentrated stages (*samāhita-bhūmi*), which sever the higher afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for "middling grade," it is as follows:
The mundane wholesome states of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and their untainted counterparts (*anāsrava*) can sever intermediate afflictions;
however, superior supramundane wholesome roots do not sever afflictions.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that various wholesome dharmas may arise through the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and so forth:
Jingyun: If, in this present life, one diligently cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) until it reaches the highest degree, it is called the power of application (*prayogabala*).
Alternatively, if it has reached the highest degree because of repeated cultivation over many previous lives, it is called the power of habituation (*vāsanābala*).
The power of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bala*) is established by virtue of its beginningless character.

The power of field and person (*kṣetra-pudgala-bala*) is established because the arising of superior goodness through giving to the supreme fields, such as the Three Jewels, is due to the exertion of the person.
The power of purity (*viśuddhi-bala*) is established as being of the highest grade because it arises based on that body which is purified through the departure from desire.
Master Ji says:
"All wholesome minds belonging to the two upper realms, as well as the wholesome,
untainted minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), which grasp at existence."
When the sixth root of goodness arises, it relies upon eight kinds of things;
the first three are merit, namely:
giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
One cultivates these four immeasurables.
The latter three are wisdoms,
namely those of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "other cultivations," this refers to all other forms of cultivation apart from the four immeasurables;
these are precisely the wholesome qualities of the stages conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) and the stages of discernment (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Seventh is discernment (*pravicaya*),
which consists of entering the stages of seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning;
it is the discernment of the principles of truth (*satya*) regarding both the established (*vyavasthāpita*) and the non-established (*avyavasthāpita*).
The eighth is the gathering of sentient beings,
which constitutes the practice of benefiting others;
it should be understood that herein, one relies on the matters as they have been explained according to what is appropriate for each case.
The preceding roots of goodness are summarized by way of eight matters;
from "or in the present life" onwards,
it clarifies their benefits.
If that practitioner, whether in this present life or in a future life, becomes defiled in mind by any kind of greed, hatred, or evil view, they shall,
by relying on the eight bases to cultivate the remedies such as generosity and ethical discipline, ensure that they no longer associate with those defiled states.
The seventh clarifies the distinctions among the wholesome (*kuśala*).
There may be one type up to ten types, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
First, the wholesome is so designated because it is generally characterized by the sense of being blameless (*anavadya*), thereby distinguishing it from the unwholesome and other categories.

The second refers to those acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) and those produced through application (*prāyogika*), and so forth. The third refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*samprayoga*), and origination (*samutthāna*).
This continues up to the fifteenth [category], which consists of five types of tenfold gateways for the increase of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).

Regarding the first [of these]:
because the measure of the aggregate as a whole and its individual parts applied to the *nirodhasatya* (truth of cessation) is inconsistent.
As stated in the *Vibhāṣā*,
the subsequent exposition of the Four Noble Truths consists of six sections;
the first clarifies the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).
Second, the sequence of the truths;
third, the meaning of the truths;
fourth, the differentiation of the two truths based on the four truths.
The fifth clarifies the knowledge of abandonment, realization, and cultivation;
the sixth clarifies the clear observation of the truths.
Regarding the first of these, there are three parts.
First, the explanation of the sixteen aspects;
second, the explanation of the ten aspects;
third, the explanation of how the three knowledges and the sixteen aspects subsume the three gates of liberation.
Regarding the preceding section:
each of those four truths has four aspects; the four aspects of the truth of suffering serve as the antidotes for the four inversions, and so forth.
Jing said:
Regarding the first line treating the first inversion:
impermanence treats the inversion of permanence.
Regarding the next line treating the next two inversions: the practice of suffering treats the inversion of pleasure.
Once one knows this to be suffering, one immediately knows it to be impure;
thus, the remaining inversions of purity are also eliminated.
As for the statement that "the latter two practices remedy the latter inversion," [this refers to the following:]
The practice of the contemplations on emptiness and non-self serves to counteract the inversion of self-grasping.
Master Ji said:
The first line serves as the antidote to the first [point],
meaning that suffering eliminates the perception of pleasure in form.
Impermanence serves as the antidote to the second.
This refers to the conceit that the body is pure and the mind is permanent.
The latter two practices counteract one [conceit] each:
emptiness and non-self counteract the conceit of a self.
Furthermore, the first line on impermanence treats the mind as permanent;
suffering treats the body as pleasant and pure, and the perception of pleasure is inverted.
The remainder is the same as above.
This differs from the sequence of the four inversions presented in the previous fascicle.
Why does asceticism serve as the antidote to the two types of wrong views?
It is because non-Buddhists, through their adherence to views and precepts (*dṛṣṭi-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), cling to these as superior causes for purity.
Because greed arises toward what is superior,
both of these [preceding] eighth [factors] are greed;
in order to eliminate this, [the following is taught].
Thus, the unification of suffering, asceticism, and the removal of pleasure and purity refers precisely to the two attachments regarding views and precepts (*dṛṣṭi-śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Regarding the statement that the four [afflictions] below "origination" exist because there are four kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), etc.:
Jingyun: The four types of craving constitute the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Because these four cravings constitute the essence of the Truth of Origination, one contemplates them through the four aspects of origination.

This is based on the general correspondence of the four numbers; one establishes the four aspects of the origin (*samudaya*) as "the cause that brings about accumulation" and "the condition that gives rise to accumulation.
One must not say, for example, "the cause is the contemplation of craving for certain formations," or "the condition is the contemplation of craving for certain formations," and so forth.
Because each of those four types of craving possesses the fourfold principle of cause, accumulation, arising, and condition.
Question: The *Maulī Bhūmi* clarifies the essential nature of the three perversions of mind, thought, and view.
In general, it is observed that both [types of craving] possess the four inversions;
however, while the inversion of mind consists of craving for pleasure and purity alone,
this present passage establishes their distinction based on the specific variations of craving for permanence, pleasure, self, and purity.
Since this is a perversion of mind that extends to both the existence of a self and permanence,
why is it said to consist only of pleasure and purity? The explanation is as follows:
Although craving is associated with four types of perversions,
because the mind is attached to pleasure and purity,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Local Section) states that its mental perversion consists solely of pleasure and purity.
Now, taking both the light and the heavy together, all four types are fully explained.
Regarding the first point, "establishing craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) and so forth with craving as the condition":
because that [craving] constantly takes craving as its condition, one establishes craving for future retribution as "craving for future existence."
With craving for the second pleasure as its condition,
one clings to and does not relinquish objects currently obtained;
this establishes craving accompanied by joy and lust.
Based on the third [type of craving], which has purity as its object,
there is the craving for longing for this or that (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī tṛṣṇā*), because one pursues purity regarding objects not yet attained.
Based on the craving for self as the final condition, craving is established.
The remaining three types of craving all carry distinct names:
namely, craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*), craving accompanied by delight and greed (*nandī-rāga-sahagatā tṛṣṇā*), and craving for various delights (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī tṛṣṇā*).
Only this craving, being designated simply as "craving," is therefore called "exclusive craving.
It should be understood that this craving follows after one's own personal existence.
It is taught that craving is known to constantly defile the manifest body;
therefore, it is said to "follow and pursue the self-substance.
Furthermore, what is meant by craving? It refers to that which is intimate with the self-substance and seeks to conceal and protect it.
This clarifies solitary craving.
Craving manifests as attachment toward one's own body, and through that bodily manifestation,
it gives rise to concealment and protection.
In summary:
craving for future existence seeks one's own self-body,
while the remaining two cravings cling to the five sense objects of the present and the future.
Tai said: "I love standing alone; this is what I take as the essence of love.
Therefore, it is called 'Solitary Love' (Duke Ai)."
Second, in the explanation of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*),
the text is divided into four parts.
First, the ten practices are listed in general, followed by a brief explanation of two of them.
Second, the ten practices are subsumed within the three types of suffering;
third, the eight sufferings are subsumed within the three types of suffering;
fourth, the four sufferings are subsumed within the eight practices.
Regarding the initial statement, "As already recorded in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* concerning the ten aspects of destruction and so forth," Jing says:
"As stated in [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] thirty-four."
The ten modes of practice subsume the four lower modes of suffering;
furthermore, among these four modes, the characteristic of the truth of suffering—
namely, the mode of impermanence— is subsumed within five categories.
First, the aspect of change;
second, the aspect of disintegration;
third, the aspect of separation.
Fourth is the practice of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Fifth is the practice of integration.
These ascetic practices are subsumed within three types of practice.
1. The practice of fetters and bonds;
2. The practice of non-differentiated craving;
3. The practice of lack of stability.
The practice of emptiness is subsumed within a single practice,
namely, the practice of non-apprehension.
The practice of selflessness is subsumed within a single practice.
This refers to the practice of non-mastery.
As for the phrase in the present text, "how is it that there is the practice of non-apprehension?":
this cites the practice of non-apprehension as elucidated therein to reveal the practice of emptiness.
That is to say: there are only the faculties and only the objects; there is only the aggregate of form and only the feeling produced by it;
there is only the establishment of the aggregate of feeling produced by the faculties;
and there is only the mind produced by those [faculties].
There is only the aggregate of consciousness produced from the sense faculties and their objects;
there is only the conceiving of a self and the notion of "I";
and there is only the aggregate of perception conceiving of "self" and "what belongs to self."
There is only the one who conceives of a self and holds the view of a self;
there is only the aggregate of formations that can conceive of a self and hold the view of a self;
there is only the conceptual proliferation of verbal expressions regarding "self" and "mine."
There is only the conceptual construction that gives rise to the verbal proliferation of the discourse on "self.
Next, the practice of non-mastery is cited to subsume the practice of non-self. Jī says:
There is only the conceptualization of a self and the notion of "I," as well as the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) consisting of the verbal proliferation of the seventh category;
for when perception gives rise to the false conceptualization of a self, it is most capable of falsely grasping at signs (nimitta).
Second, regarding the explanation of how the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are subsumed within the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkha*),
Jing states: "This refers to the practice of bondage (*bandhana-caryā*)."
It is an unattractive practice,
an insecure practice, and is subsumed under the practice of suffering.
It should be understood that the distress arising from the binding aspect of formations and their subsequent disintegration constitutes the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
Suffering produced by the disintegration of conditions necessarily arises due to bondage;
for one who is free from desire, such distress is immediately eliminated.
The opponent says:

"Since the very destruction of pleasant feeling is itself called the suffering of change, why is it necessary to establish the suffering of change by means of the activity of fetters? Since we do not hold this position, [the text] says, 'not merely through transformation and destruction,' and so forth."
This refers to a person who has attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and has abandoned sorrow through detachment from desire;
for even when encountering the destruction of pleasure, they do not give rise to sorrow or affliction.
This is due to the existence of fetters.
The arising of sorrow due to the destruction of what one is bound to is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
If the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are themselves destroyed, that is suffering; this is called the suffering of change.
Because the destruction of conditions that give rise to sorrow and affliction is termed the meaning of "suffering due to change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
As for that which is subsumed under the aspect of being undesirable,
it is called "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) because the feeling of suffering takes suffering itself as its intrinsic characteristic.

Furthermore, because the objects that give rise to this root of craving and their associated phenomena accord with painful feeling, they are called the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
This refers to what is "unpleasant to practice" (*aniṣṭa-vipāka*).
Taking all that is associated with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) together with its attendants as "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*);
and because it is subsumed under the mode of being unstable (*aniścaritratā*),

the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)— together with its equanimity (*upekṣā*) and those factors conducive to this equanimity— is the essence of the "suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
Because they are burdened by the heaviness of *nirvāṇa* and the heaviness of the two types of suffering,
which follow them from beginning to end, they cannot proceed with stability;
that is suffering.
It is called "suffering in conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Ji says:
This means that pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is not only termed suffering at the time it is destroyed by its opposite.
Since pleasant feelings themselves undergo transformation and the craving they produce constitutes the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*),
those who have attained the third fruit and beyond are not harmed even when encountering such contrary transformations, because they are free from craving.
Because there is no cause for celebration,
one knows that the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) applies to both types:
first, the intrinsic nature of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
"The second refers to the time when pleasure undergoes transformation and decay;
this is the intended meaning here.

As the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* says:
"If among this assembly there are those who have not yet crossed the ocean of suffering,

Those who have already crossed the ocean of suffering thought to themselves: "How swift was the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One!
By this they realized that those possessed of afflictions [must likewise pass away].
There is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

at times of separation from what is loved and the failure to obtain what is sought, the suffering of suffering also arises;
therefore, the first seven sufferings are all subsumed under the suffering of suffering.
Those who do not diligently cultivate purification regarding the afflictions will have their minds—
where purity and defilement coexist— corrupted by grasping;
this corruption is itself suffering.

Furthermore, because greed can transform and corrupt the mind, causing one to experience future suffering,
it is called the suffering of change.

the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) are formations (*saṃskāra*), because these formations are accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and lack stability.

therefore, these first seven sufferings are also termed the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
Below, two phrases from a sutra are cited as proof.
Regarding "the first entry into a mind subject to transformation and decay":
when the Buddha perceives that sentient beings have given rise to desire,
he immediately records their state by saying they have entered a mind subject to transformation and decay.
This constitutes what is comprised by the suffering of change within the afflictions that are pure and subtle.
Furthermore, from the passage beginning with "Again,
having said this," it is demonstrated that those who have not yet abandoned desire give rise to grief and distress when encountering adverse circumstances of change.
Thus, one knows that afflictions constitute the reality of suffering.
Fourth, it clarifies how the four types of suffering are subsumed within the eight aspects.
Among these:
Jingyun says that the eight [factors] constitute the eightfold path,
which together with the four listed here mutually encompass one another.
Regarding the mutual inclusion of the first suffering among the initial practices:
among the eight sufferings, the first, the suffering of birth,
is identical in essence— neither broader nor narrower— to the suffering of birth within the four [truths].
Therefore, they are mutually inclusive.
Next, regarding the three modes of conduct that are subsumed under the second characteristic of suffering:
the three modes of old age, sickness, and death are subsumed within this internal condition of suffering.
Next, regarding the inclusion of the three lines with the third characteristic of suffering:
the three lines—association with the disliked, separation from the beloved, and failure to obtain what one seeks—are included within the characteristic of suffering conditioned by external factors.
The final activity of the five aggregates of clinging is subsumed under this fourth aspect of suffering, namely, the state of heavy dysfunction (*dausthulya*).
Tai [Sheng] says:
The arising and ceasing of the eight sufferings are precisely what is called the "eight aspects.

Regarding the statement that the four aspects of the previously explained Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) should be understood as the four specific sufferings that constitute the present result of arising: [this refers to the following].

"Seeking what one later comes to love gives rise to this suffering;
being attached to it alone gives rise to this internal suffering."
The craving that accompanies joy and greed, and the craving for various objects of longing, arise; conditioned by these, external suffering arises.

This present life is not a distinct life from others;
furthermore, considering the concealment of his father,
it is somewhat difficult to enumerate his successive births.
Third, the explanation of how the sixteen aspects subsume the three doors of liberation.
First, the mutual inclusion of these aspects is clarified; subsequently, their sequential order is distinguished through a series of questions and answers.
Regarding the initial inquiry: "Of these sixteen aspects, how many are the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? and so forth.
It is subsumed within eight gates,
as recorded in the twelfth fascicle; the details are distinguished below in the questions and answers.
The meaning of the question is that prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
one must first contemplate impermanence (*anityatā*).
It is constantly the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Subsequently, upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one abides in the mark of non-self (*anātman-lakṣaṇa*);
this mark of non-self is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Question: Among the gates of liberation, why is the gate of emptiness mentioned first rather than the gate of wishlessness?
Answer: This is because prior to the path of vision (darśanamārga), [the practitioner first realizes emptiness].

In the initial cultivation of skillful means, one first gives rise to the three samādhis of impermanence, suffering, and wishlessness; subsequently, one cultivates the samādhi of emptiness regarding selflessness.
Its essence consists in cultivating that emptiness by relying upon non-interruption.
Furthermore, from non-self one gives rise to the contemplation of impermanence;
based upon that emptiness, one cultivates wishlessness.
Wishlessness and emptiness—
These are cultivated sequentially and reciprocally.
Regarding the fact that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) was mentioned first among the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*),
this is based on having already attained the practice of the contemplation of emptiness and non-self (*anātman*).
Next, [one contemplates] suffering, impermanence, and so forth;
therefore, emptiness is taught first and wishlessness is taught afterward.
Below this, the second section clarifies the sequence of the Truths (satya).
There are two successive expositions.
In the first exposition, the principle is presented first, followed by the analogy.
"By virtue of which this is suffering, with this as the final and that as the first," etc., means:
by virtue of oppression it is suffering;
the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is the first.
It is suffering because it is like the truth of origination,
for there must be a cause for there to be a fruit;
it is bliss because of the realization of cessation.
Regarding the path for the cessation of pleasure,
in the second section, the Dharma is elucidated by means of an analogy.
This is precisely the sequence of practice.
Regarding the meaning of the Threefold Truth, Jing says:
Regarding the meaning of "the characteristics as they have been described are not abandoned":
true suffering cannot be made into happiness, and so on,
up to the fact that the path leading to the cessation of suffering is truly the authentic path.
This refers to "truth" (*satya*) in its actual sense;
thus, the meaning of "abandoning" is the meaning of "truth.
Because one reaches the ultimate state of purification by contemplating this, it is the meaning of "truth."
That which can produce non-erroneous awakening is called "truth" (*satya*).

To say that it "establishes the meaning of the three truths" means it establishes the three types of beneficial purposes: knowing suffering, abandoning the origin [of suffering], and realizing cessation.
Ce says: Furthermore, "truth" (satya) has two meanings.
First, the meaning that all dharmas do not abandon their own nature (svabhāva) is the meaning of truth.
Therefore, the *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* states:
"The Buddha taught that the Four Noble Truths must not be altered;
secondly, they have the meaning of being able to give rise to pure wisdom."
The fourth [section] distinguishes the two truths based on the four truths.
The intended meaning herein is that the two truths of cessation and the path, as well as the ultimate truths of suffering and its origin, [are so designated].

Because these three types of sensation and so forth, by virtue of their common characteristic, are all of a single flavor of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), they constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If explained according to their specific distinctions, the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) is [the truth of] suffering, while the others are [the truths of] origination and so forth.
It is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) precisely by virtue of its specific nature.
There are four types of conventional truth, as in the seventy-fourth [verse]:
first, the conventional within conventional truth.
As it is said, the names "bed," "seat," "army," "forest," and "jar" are worldly conventions (*loka-saṃvṛti*).
Second is the conventional [truth] of reasoning (*yukti-saṃvṛti*),
which refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, etc., as conventional [truths] by way of reasoning.
Third is the conventional attainment,
which refers to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Fourth is the ultimate conventional.
This refers to the teaching that there is no self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*),
and so forth. Herein, according to the principle of worldly convention,
this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Due to the distinction of their intrinsic natures,
one should know by analogy that the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) in the West is also fourfold.
First, the ultimate truth of reasoning (yuktisatyaparamārtha).
The first refers to the principles of the aggregates and so forth, which are not suchness itself.
The second is the ultimate truth as realization,
namely, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Third is the ultimate ultimate,
which refers to entering true contemplation and the single flavor of suchness.
Fourth is the conventional ultimate.
This refers to contemplating all things as having the characteristic of suffering.
Herein, this is called "ultimate" (paramārtha) in terms of the conventional and ultimate teachings.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*:
Each of the Four Noble Truths possesses the significance of the two truths.
For example, when humans, devas, men, women, and so forth are described as suffering, this refers to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) of the truth of suffering.
That suffering is impermanent, empty, and non-self is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
As it is said, that parents can give birth to and nourish [a child] and so forth is the conventional truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*);
that there is a cause for origination and conditions for arising is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As it is said, that which is like a city or a garden, a place for wandering and observing, is called the conventional truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
To speak of cessation as being correct, wonderful, and transcendent is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
To speak of it as being like a stone city, like a flower, or like water is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) of the path.
Preparatory application (prayoga) is directed toward this ultimate truth.
That which he calls the conventional corresponds here to the first gate of the conventional;
that which he calls the ultimate corresponds here to the second, the ultimate.
This is clearly understood within the fifth [chapter], concerning the abandonment, realization, and cultivation.

Therefore, the thorough knowledge of suffering is itself the thorough knowledge of its origin. Cè states:

Its cause refers to faith prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) which is still with outflows (*sāsrava*).

If that is so, is that which is co-existent with it the same as that which is mixed with it?
To explain this separately now:
definitive wisdom (*niścaya-jñāna*) consists of three types: the truth of knowledge (*jñāna-satya*), the limit-of-reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the complete realization (*abhisamaya*).
Because all arise conditioned by the truths;
and as for their cause, it is the contemplative realization (cintā-abhisamaya),
because this wisdom is the cause of the truths.

[it refers to the supreme state of the untainted].

why were wisdom, the truths, and so forth mentioned previously?

the clear realization that takes the truths as its object refers to the knowledge of the truths (jñānasatya), the limit-of-reality (bhūtakoṭi), and so forth.
The others are not actual direct realization (*abhisamaya*).

If they are called "direct realization" because they are causes for the direct realization through reflection (*cintā-abhisamaya*), or if they are designated as "direct realization" due to their association with faith and understanding, [they are so named only figuratively].
The precepts are called "insight" (abhisamaya) in the sense of being equivalent to the existence of suffering and so forth;
they are not the actual insight itself.
Therefore, I now answer by skipping the sequence and leaping over it.
Because it first correctly manifests the essence of contemplation,
as stated elsewhere:
"First, one clarifies volition, faith, and so forth."

rather, its characteristic is that the essence of the knowledge cultivated on the path of seeing is contaminated (sāsrava).

"All seeds of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the stage of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*)."

It is faith associated with cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
