that faith is the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma.
The wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) stands at the head of the three types of wisdom.
The wisdom accomplished during the interval between gaining conviction and practicing accordingly is called the "clear realization through faith" (śraddhābhisamaya).
This is based on the emergence of the essence of faith and contemplation occurring simultaneously.
Jizang says: "If one were to rely on the actual state of affairs, this faith would encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
However, here we speak only in terms of the superior, uncontaminated kind."
Why is it called "wisdom"? Because within the tainted (*sāsrava*) states, it is spoken of as the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
and because prior to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the mind that first takes the teachings as its object is preceded by the wisdom of hearing.
In this context, the mention of "outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*) discourse is intended to include the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). If that is so,
why is the wisdom derived from hearing not established separately?
The commentary states:
If one relies on the initial condition of the Truths (satya), faith must serve as the primary guide;
thus, for those in whom faith is predominant, the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) becomes supreme, because it is the wisdom born of reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā) that is preeminent.
Relying solely on faith, reflection, and the wisdom of hearing, these are subsumed within faith (*śraddhā*).

Cultivation and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); the superior among them is comprised within knowledge (*jñāna*), the truths (*satya*), and so forth.
What about those with outflows (*sāsrava*)? As explained regarding the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
because they do not increase [the roots of goodness], they are also included within faith (*śraddhā*).
This has not yet been seen in the texts;
it is taken as scriptural evidence based on the wisdom derived from hearing and the faith of conviction.
Thus, its essence consists precisely of these two factors: hearing and conviction.
However, although the initial increase of faith and understanding follows the discourse on faith,
here the discussion regarding knowledge, the truths, and so forth refers exclusively to their first attainment during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Nevertheless, the subsequent sections also include the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and other stages.
The stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is collectively termed "ultimate contemplation" (*niṣṭhābhiniścaya*).

Regarding the statement in the third [section] on the present that one does not perform formal vows (*saṃvara*), this refers to the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the path (*mārga-saṃvara*).
By the power of this ethical discipline,
one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the three evil destinies, such that they will never arise again.
Within the fourth clear realization (*abhisamaya*),...
First the inquiry,
next the explanation,
and finally the conclusion.
In the explanation,
first the essence of the contemplation is presented,
and subsequently it is analyzed according to its meaning.
Regarding the preceding section, Jingyun states:
"This refers to the fact that within the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), one has previously accumulated the provisions (*sambhāra*) to the point of complete perfection."
This distant preparation (*dūrasādhana*) is termed "provision" (*sambhāra*) when it exists at the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because the skillful means polish and refine the mind":
this refers to the stage of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), wherein one trains in the contemplation of the Four Truths until they gradually become clear and sharp.
This is the proximate preparation (*sāmantaka*).

Immediately following the ultimate roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that accord with the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) within the mundane realm, one emerges from the fundamental [attainment].

That is to say, immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one first enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and takes the emptiness of the person (*pudgalanairātmya*) as its object.
When one gives rise to inferior non-conceptual wisdom in accordance with the Dharma, it is called the arising of a mind that takes phenomena as its object;
this eliminates the superior-level coarse residues of the grasping at a personal self.
Next, one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena.
Just as when one gives rise to middle-grade non-conceptual wisdom,
one abandons the coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) of the superior grade of clinging to phenomena;
in the third stage, one simultaneously contemplates the two kinds of emptiness.
In accordance with the Dharma, one gives rise to non-conceptual wisdom,
which simultaneously severs the two types of grasping and the inferior-grade heavy residues (*dausthulya*).
Now, regarding these three minds:
The interpretations are not fixed.

One school asserts that the three minds constitute the true path of seeing; prior to this, one first habituates oneself through preparatory means by first contemplating the emptiness of persons, next contemplating the emptiness of phenomena, and finally contemplating the simultaneous emptiness of both.
Although there is no conceptual discrimination when one subsequently enters the path of seeing, it is understood spontaneously through the power of repeated cultivation.
First, one contemplates the emptiness of persons, just as one removes the superior grade of grasping at a person;
next, one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena, just as one removes the superior grade of grasping at phenomena.
Subsequently, one contemplates the two emptinesses simultaneously; this is the lower grade of severing a single attachment.
The second explanation states:
"The three minds are not the true path of vision."
However, prior to entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one practices the preparatory contemplation;
subsequently, upon entering the True Path of Seeing, a single moment of mind (*ekakṣaṇacitta*) suddenly severs all afflictions of dualistic grasping.
One then emerges from the True Path of Seeing.

Subsequently, within the mind of subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one contemplates the true suchness (*tathatā*) manifested by the two kinds of emptiness that have been realized, as well as the two types of grasping that have been abandoned; these three minds that arise are called the subsequent path of vision (*anvaya-darśanamārga*).
If one were to assume that true contemplation consists of three minds,
these three minds are spoken of solely from the perspective of the meaning of the single-flavored object and wisdom;
the following explains their alternative names.
The simultaneous cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā is called "dual application.
Ji quotes the Tripiṭaka Master as saying:
"To dispel the conventional designation of a sentient being."
This refers to practicing within the path of skillful means.

Regarding the statement "the mind arises with dharmas as its object," this is discussed from the perspective of the causal relationship of the mind arising in the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Because the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) does not separately perform such conceptual observations as those regarding sentient beings,
the Ācārya Sāgaramegha of Nālandā Monastery explains these three minds as not being based on the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
This is also the practice of the two vehicles. Why is this so?
Because one first contemplates the dharmas individually as being without self, one thus cultivates the contemplation of the practice of non-self.
The first is called the elimination of the conventional designation of sentient beings;
next, through the practice of emptiness, one eliminates the conventional designations of "mine" and "dharmas," thereby removing attachment to what belongs to a self.
This is called the second provisional designation of the dharma.
The third [provisional designation] concerns the self and the dharmas belonging to the self;
it involves repeatedly contemplating the inferior degree of emptiness regarding the self and what belongs to the self.
This is called the "universal elimination of the two types of designation.
However, for the present purpose, we take the Mahāyāna alone as superior.
Regarding this treatise, the masters of the Western Regions have three distinct explanations.
The first interpretation:
the initial mind correctly severs the superior grade of clinging to a personal self;
the subsequent mind correctly severs the middle grade of clinging to phenomena.
The medium grade of clinging to persons is countered by the [medium] name; the superior grade may be understood accordingly.
The final mind severs the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the former two grades.
Therefore, among the three moments of mind, the first two are called the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*),
and the last one is called the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is the second interpretation.
The two types of grasping—grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena—each have two grades.

With the first moment of mind, one abandons the first grade of grasping at persons; with the subsequent moment of mind, one abandons the first grade of grasping at phenomena; and with the final moment of mind, one simultaneously abandons the second grades of both types of grasping.
However, because of the correspondence between person and dharma,
the first is called the superior grade and the next is called the middling grade;
furthermore, there is a fourth mind called the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The third explanation:
There are two types of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
First, the true path of seeing, which suddenly realizes the two emptinesses and suddenly abandons the two obstacles.

The two types of the path of vision—namely, the three moments and the sixteen moments—are the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that re-attests to the abandonment of the afflictions severed by the path of vision; this is a provisional designation for their abandonment.
Within this context, if one enters the signless path of vision (*animitta-darśanamārga*), [the afflictions are abandoned].
Next, the three minds emerge;
when those of the two vehicles enter the path of seeing,
the sixteen moments of mind emerge.
The second [section], the analysis according to the meaning, consists of five statements.
First: "It should be known that these various minds take as their object only the non-established truth (apratiṣṭhita-satya)."

One should know that although the three moments of mind in the path of seeing are described in terms of conventional expression as taking the person, the provisional, and phenomena such as dharmas as objects,
in reality they take only true suchness— the non-established realm— as their object. Second,
it is said that the first two moments of mind are associated with dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), while the third moment of mind is associated with subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Dharma) states at the ninth [section] that all three minds are "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*), because they equally contemplate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

This treatise [the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*] considers the third [mind], which is the knowledge of the true suchness revealed by the simultaneous contemplation of the two emptinesses, to be of the same category as the first two minds, which contemplate them individually.
Therefore, it is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Third, regarding the phrase "furthermore, precisely by the power of this mind": Jing says:
By the power of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is able to give rise to the second, the path of seeing of characteristics (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*).
The wisdoms that perceive the suffering and other aspects of the eight truths—both lower and higher—arise therein.
This path of seeing of characteristics is called "the second" because it arises subsequent to the true path of seeing.
Having emerged from the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates this contemplation;
it is called the "contemplation at the limit" (*prāntakoṭika-abhisamaya*). It takes the characteristics of the established truths (*vyavasthāpanasatya*) as its object.
This is called the Path of Vision of Names and Characteristics (*nāmanimitta-darśanamārga*).
Tái asks: "Why do the enumerations of the [defilements] seen differ?"
This is because the practitioner gives rise to a distinct contemplation that differs [from others]. As a sūtra states:
"Nirvāṇa is the true jewel."
Sentient beings enter by way of various doors.
Ce (Ceshi) says:
"The sixteen moments of mind arise because of the three [initial] minds."
It should be understood that a single person brings forth these three minds.

Fourth, it is said that when these aforementioned three minds, together with the categories of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, are able to realize the cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), [this constitutes the fourth].
The realization of the unconditioned state wherein the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing have been extinguished.
Regarding the fifth point, which states that one can attain the supramundane path that eternally extinguishes all afflictions along with their underlying bases, Jing says:

By the power of the path of seeing, one is able to lead to the final stage of the path of training—the diamond-like samādhi—which eternally extinguishes the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
Once these afflictions are exhausted, rebirth will no longer occur;
this is termed the "basis" (*vastu*).
The dharma that extinguishes birth and death brings the fruit of exhaustion to sudden completion,
serving as the supramundane path. Jing said:
This refers only to the complete exhaustion [of defilements] at the stage of the Path of Vision (darśanamārga),
not to the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).
As for the "basis" (āśrayavastu):
This refers to the five aggregates being summoned by the afflictions of the path of seeing;
alternatively, this is the diamond-like mind within the fifth clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
First, the essential nature of the culmination-insight (*prānta-abhisamaya*) is correctly established;
subsequently, its distinctions are clarified in relation to the fourth insight.
Within the former [section]:
First the question,
next the explanation,
and finally the conclusion.
In the commentary, there are seven statements. The first says:
"That which is called the subsequently attained wisdom following this clear realization is termed 'wisdom at the limit of clear realization' (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna*)."
This explains its essential nature.
That is to say, the path of vision consisting of images arises from the final stage of true contemplation;
this is called the "culminating clear observation."
Regarding the second point, "it should be known that this wisdom," and so forth:
this distinguishes the stages [of realization],
namely the contemplative observation of limits.
It manifests immediately after the third true mind.
Regarding the phrase "taking as its object the wisdom that previously observed [phenomena] in past lives," this distinguishes the door of the objects of cognition.
Regarding this, there are two explanations.

One states that the objects of observation are the afflictions of the desire realm and the two upper realms (the form and formless realms)—namely, the truths of suffering and its origin—which were previously examined during the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, there are two, namely the objects of the higher established truths, which are the truths of cessation and the path;
these serve as the two types of predominance (*adhipati*).
Another interpretation states:
It is called "previously observed" because it takes as its object the preceding Path of True Vision (*darśanamārga*).
Because it transcends the Path of True Vision,
it takes as its objects the four noble truths established as superior within both the lower and upper stages, as well as all that exists therein.
For this reason, one should know that this accords with the meaning of "superior friend.
That person says: the first two minds take the persons and phenomena of the lower realms as objects of clinging;
the third mind takes the persons and phenomena of the two upper realms as objects of clinging.
Therefore, it is called "the elimination of extremes.
This is because this [path] is established as the path of insight (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, this master explains:
When one abandons the inferior grade of the grasping at a person (*pudgalagrāha*), one also abandons the inferior grade of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
When one abandons the middle grade of the grasping at phenomena, one also abandons the middle grade of the grasping at a person.
Here, because of this elliptical abbreviation, the grasping at a person is designated as the inferior grade and the grasping at phenomena as the middle grade.
This is discussed solely in terms of the grasping mind;
therefore, it is spoken of as merely one.
Furthermore, the distinction between "lower" and "upper" is made simply by comparing the person with the dharmas.
It is not that each individual constitutes its own superior or inferior. Why is this so?
Because they are born from the same single seed.
Therefore, they are designated as inferior or superior in relation to one another.
Fourth, regarding "that which resembles the knowledge of dharma and subsequent knowledge," this is the section distinguishing between the genuine and the counterfeit.
Prior to the three moments of mind in the path of seeing, there are two true dharma-knowledges and a third true subsequent knowledge.

Now, within this contemplation of characteristics, the four dharma-patience and four dharma-knowledges collectively take as their object the essential nature of the eight truths of the lower and upper realms.
They are called "resembling dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna-anvaya*).
The four anvaya-acceptances (*anvayakṣānti*) and the four anvaya-knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) take the preceding dharma-acceptances (*dharmakṣānti*) and dharma-knowledges as their objects;
they are called "resembling anvaya-knowledge" (*anvayajñāna-anvaya*).
Regarding the statement that "the five clouds are comprised within the conventional and penetrate both the mundane and the supramundane":
this is said in contrast to non-conceptual wisdom;
therefore, subsequent wisdom is termed conventional wisdom.
Its essence is untainted, and thus it is called "transcending the world";
yet because it arises by taking worldly phenomena as its object, it is also called "worldly.
It is for this reason that [it is so designated].
It encompasses both the mundane and the supramundane.
The sixth [point] states, "This is that which is subsequently attained after supramundane wisdom," which explains the name of "subsequently attained wisdom" (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
This also clarifies the sequence.
Regarding the seventh point, "In accordance with the sequence, two kinds of knowledge arise for each truth," and so forth:
the knowledge that confirms [the truth] is *kṣānti* (receptivity).
This is the wisdom of one with definitive knowledge. Tai says:
"Based on this treatise, one contemplates the Four Truths of each of the three realms separately as the Eight Truths Contemplation."
This differs from the contemplation of the eight truths in the Abhidharma.
As the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Commentary) cites and explains:
"Within the three minds, the first two minds separately contemplate the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena—within the desire realm."
Thereafter, with a single mind, one contemplates the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) throughout the upper realms.

Upon reaching the third moment of mind, because persons and phenomena have been universally eliminated, this is termed the "sixteenfold contemplation of truth" (*ṣoḍaśākāra-satyadhyāna*) based on that universal elimination.
Thus, the upper and lower realms are contemplated separately.
Therefore, one should know that the three minds are discussed as superior friends.
However, the Abhidharma-śāstra distinguishes the characteristics of these three minds by way of their respective objects—self and others.
Thus, there are sixteen contemplations.
The eight conditions are the grasper, and the eight conditions are the grasped.
Cè (Cè) describes the Tripiṭaka Master’s words, asking: "Why do these two treatises differ?"
Because the paths to entering nirvāṇa are not one but many:
some sentient beings, relying on the Abhidharma treatises, perform sixteen contemplations by way of observing the grasped and the grasper;
others, relying on the Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, perform sixteen contemplations by way of observing the truths of the ascending and descending orders.
Within the second section, which distinguishes the differences, there are three successive expositions.

In the sixth exposition, clarifying the distinctions among what is grasped, it states: "There is no purely mundane path that can eternally eradicate the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)," and so forth.
Jingyun says:
This refers to the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which is exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*) and is purely mundane.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the "Explanation of the Reasons" that "one is because it was previously practiced," [it means that the subsequent knowledge of the two vehicles was cultivated during their training].
The subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) after the path of cultivation is manifested as the path of seeing with signs;
it is called "previously practiced.

One must not say that the knowledge cultivated at the limit of seeing is now arising in the stage of cultivation and is thus called "previously obtained," because that [knowledge] is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and is therefore not termed "subsequent knowledge."
Regarding the present position that the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) permeates both mundane and supramundane aspects:
as for the phrase "because it clings to [them]," this clinging to aspects refers to the two types of clinging of the manas.
When entering true contemplation (*bhūtadhyāna*), the two types of grasping do not arise;
now, upon emerging from that truth, the grasping for appearances arises again.
Consequently, the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) cannot subdue or eliminate the phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the three realms.
For these three reasons, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not permanently destroyed.
Tái says: "This distinguishes [this wisdom] from the reason why subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does not sever them."
It is called a purely mundane path because it takes conditioned phenomena as its object;

it is not designated as supramundane on account of the meaning of being untainted (*anāsrava*). As for the phrase "because it has been practiced before": [it refers to having been cultivated in previous lives].
It is called "formerly practiced" (pūrvābhyasta) subsequent to non-conceptual wisdom.
Furthermore, this object-condition, which is signless and non-conceptual wisdom, is formerly practiced;
although it is of a contaminated nature, they are similar in kind.
The reason is that it is led by the grasping at the characteristics of tainted consciousness;
consequently, even subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) comes to possess characteristics,
and so forth, as explained at length.
Another interpretation is that the purely mundane path consists of outflow-tainted wisdom (sāsrava-jñāna) and is incapable of severing afflictions.
If this were the case, then...
What is the purpose of including this here?
It is intended merely to distinguish that subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does not sever the afflictions;
it is not referring to contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*).
Regarding the sixth clear observation (*abhisamaya*), Jing says:
"That which is said to be 'exclusively supramundane' refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)."
That which is common to both the mundane and supramundane is subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
This clarifies that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) have as their essence the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional.
Regarding the definitive and permanent abandonment of afflictions within the present life, this explains the meaning of the knowledge of exhaustion.
Regarding the certainty that in future lives all bases of existence will be eternally extinguished:
one would otherwise give rise to afflictions, karma, and the resultant realms of rebirth.
The fact that these bases do not arise at all is the explanation of the meaning of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
This section explains that the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) pertain to both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Therefore, one cannot say that the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising take only such [conventional] objects as "my births are exhausted" as their cognitive domain.
It does not speak of "exhaustion" and so forth.
Of the three sections within the preceding "Gate of the Mutual Inclusion of the Aggregates of Truths," two have already been concluded.
From here below begins the third section: Refuting the Erroneous and Distinguishing the Correct.
Within this, first the erroneous attachments are refuted,
and subsequently the correct principle is demonstrated.
In the former section, there are two parts.
First, three chapters are raised;
later, they will be analyzed individually.
What are these three chapters?
First, the three truths of a brahmin;
second, abiding in the three faults;
third, falling into the category of those who are not true brahmins.
Within the section on specific distinctions,
there are three parts. The first part is further divided into three sections.
First, the three locations are listed by way of inquiry;
next, they are explained individually;
finally, they are summarized.
The explanation consists of three parts.
First, regarding the maintenance of life, the preliminary means for maintaining life are distinguished;
subsequently, the faults of enjoyment are clarified.
Within the preceding section, three phrases are further distinguished:
first, the bestowing of blessings;
second, the offering of praise.
The third life-narrative states:
within the verses of incantation and aspiration there are two phrases;
the verses of praise contain three phrases.
The introduction consists of three phrases.
Within the second section on cultivating merit, there are three phrases.
The first proclaims that one may perform sacrifices for merit by slaughtering immeasurable sentient beings.
Second, one obtains the fruit of the eternal realm of Brahmā through sacrifice.
Third, because of sacrifices, there arises much and narrow gain and honor, leading to mutual contempt later on;
this is established as the third fruit.
First the analysis,
then the conclusion;
below, a summary of the three points.
In the second section,
first the three faults are interrogated and listed;
subsequently, they are explained in sequence.
Among these, the first examines the faults of speech:
namely, uttering words of flattery,
benedictions, praise, and formal introductions for the sake of maintaining one's livelihood.
Furthermore, they exhaustively engage in false speech and frivolous chatter.
Within their cultivation of merit, they advocate for the extensive slaughter of living beings to establish sacrificial altars as fields of merit,
claiming that through such sacrificial killing one attains the fruit of eternal abiding and so forth.
This is also frivolous speech;
thus, it is a fault of speech.
Next, the faults of pride are distinguished.
This refers to grasping the three aforementioned bases as being truths and realities, and giving rise to pride by disparaging others.
Third, there are five distinct phrases concerning resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
First, regarding the three established bases, one does not examine their merits or faults but accepts them unilaterally.
Second, although they encounter the Buddha and his disciples' instructions, they are unable to abide correctly.
Third, regarding the comprehensive analysis of the teachings throughout the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, they are unable to abide correctly.
Fourth, they do not abide in correct practice.
Fifth, they are unable to properly abide when establishing a treatise regarding the wise bodhisattvas.
This third section concludes that, based on their evil views, they are not counted among the brahmins.
From here below is the second section, which demonstrates the correct meaning.
Within it,
first the chapter headings are presented.
The subsequent explanation.
Within this explanation,
first it clarifies that there are no three faults regarding the three locations.
The latter clarifies that [such a person] is included among the number of Brahmins in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
In the preceding middle section, it says:
"That is to say, one should not harm any sentient being."
This overturns and refutes the second [position]: that one harms living beings for the sake of cultivating merit through sacrificial offerings.
Below, it is demonstrated that this position is free from three faults:
first, regarding the stated point that one does not harm living beings, there is no fault of falsehood, as it is strictly true and without deceptive speech.
Second, not grasping at this speech as "I" and arising pride by disparaging others.
Third, regarding the fault of lack of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), there are four distinct points:
first, being able to increase wholesome dharmas through carefully examining the virtues and faults of non-harming.
Second, by means of non-harming, one is able to gather and benefit body and mind, abiding in happiness in the present life.
Third, one dwells in the perception of loving-kindness.
Fourth, regarding non-harming, rather than relying on the conduct of others, one must personally realize it through correct awakening.
Regarding the statement, "To say that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent is the second point;
the rest is as previously explained," this reverses the third established [position] wherein the celestial body (*deva-kāya*) is held to be permanent and free from the three faults.
Regarding the statement, "The third point is that all phenomena are without self; the rest is as explained before":
this reverses the first [point], which concerns sustaining life, wherein they conceive of a self and seek the requisites for that self.
For the sake of sustaining my life, I perform incantations, aspirations, praises, and introductory accounts.
The distinction here is that, within the first [category] of non-harming, it is taught that one should dwell frequently in thoughts of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
End of the Upper Part of the Fifteenth Scroll of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*.
